title: Would people even buy games when AI advances substantially from now...?
author: Tomukim
selftext:
I've been making games that I personally want to play with my friends. It takes a lot of iteration and time to get it to a point of acceptable quality (not commercial level, literally is this playable with my friends), but as AI continues to improve, I was wondering, why would people "buy" games when they AI would be able to make a game that is specifically tailored to their interest (and pretty well I assume in the future)?

Even if there's an "interesting" game out there, AI would be able to basically "copy" or adapt the game's core idea and perhaps even add modifications that would make much more enjoyable and tailored for the person. Basically AI would provide the "best game" for each person individually. So I just was thinking why would one buy a game in the future, or stretching further, if the game market would still be alive at that point. Maybe I'm too optimistic about AI can actually do and to which extent they can improve but... just wanted to share my thoughts.

comments.author: BackgroundPresence60
comments.body: It's true with more ai advancements it will kind of dilute the pool and lower the value of many things not the least of which will be games.

comments.author: TrapWasATrap
comments.body:
I think people will still buy games, but what they are paying for will change.

AI may eventually be able to generate a game tailored to one person, but a game is more than its mechanics or content. People also value shared worlds, communities, multiplayer populations, recognizable characters, competition, mod scenes, trusted creators, and the feeling that millions of other people experienced the same thing.

An AI could generate “a better version of this mechanic for me,” but it cannot automatically recreate the history, culture, friendships, status, and shared memories surrounding an established game. A personalized imitation of Minecraft is not the same thing as actually being part of Minecraft’s community.

There is also a difference between generating something and directing it well. When infinite content becomes cheap, good judgment and curation become more valuable. Most people probably will not want to constantly design every detail of their own game. They will want a strong starting world that they can then modify conversationally: “make the combat harder,” “add political factions,” “turn this into co-op,” or “generate a new campaign for our group.”

So I do not think the game market disappears. I think it shifts from selling fixed, finished packages toward selling persistent worlds, communities, characters, infrastructure, creator ecosystems, and tools for generating or modifying experiences.

The future may be less “buy this exact game and play it unchanged” and more “join this world, then let AI adapt and expand it around you.”

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
lol

I've been hearing this promise from sci-fi and tech bros since the 90s.

comments.author: theflossboss1
comments.body: I mean probably not once AI gets good enough.  There are a few open source game frameworks out there that can 1 shot most basic games like platformers or shooters.  Right now their art is pretty janky but that will change pretty fast

comments.author: bingewavecinema
comments.body:
Right now we're in a bubble where the real price of Ai is not what what we are paying for. When AI becomes it true cost, making a "good" game with prob cost 5k to 10k,

So yes people will still buy games made by good game makers.

comments.author: InsolentCoolRadio
comments.body:
People can microwave their own food, but they still go to restaurants 

If you’re serving something better than microwaved burritos this is not a real problem

Also, vibe coding a game takes time, money, and effort that exceeds what it would cost to pay $1-$70 for the equivalent game that the user can play on demand and go back to the rest of their life

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body: It isn't vibe coding if it takes effort, you are in control of what it becomes, and you can continuously develop it further.

replies.author: ThickBootyEnjoyer
replies.body: Vibe coding still takes effort. And the microwave analogy works just fine, you might not understand it.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
Typing in a prompt and repeatedly pressing a button is ridiculous effort compared to actual game development.

And a microwave doesn't prepare food for you. It only heats it. So does an oven or stove btw. I don't know why people still think of microwaves as something super advanced and mysterious and scary. They have been around aince the 70s.

comments.author: ilganeli
comments.body: I feel this, I think people will still pay for craft and beauty. Asset generation, engine design, game mechanics, all are evolving, but doesn't mean there's no more good games to be made. So many of the demos are just direct copies / clones or slop. If you make something original that has your soul in it, don't see any reason people wouldn't pay.

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body: They'd still buy them for the same reason I still buy games today. I'm a game dev by profession and I'm experienced enough to make just about any game I want, even more so with AI. I still wouldn't do it because the point of playing a game is to experience the novelty or story someone else wrote. It's no fun if you know literally every little detail of what you're playing. Likewise it's not as much fun without the shared culture around the game that appears from other people playing it, which you definitely won't get from "AI make me a game like...".

comments.author: BJGG69
comments.body:
It seems like we are pretty far off from that point as of yet. Yes, you can build games yourself with AI, but for it to be able to automate a game like Cyberpunk or RDR2, we still need a lot more advanced AI models (maybe ChatGPT 10, who knows) and a ton of compute. So for the foreseeable future, unless you want to burn a massive budget on tokens, people will be buying games. 

However, once we do get to that point, far fewer people will be willing to spend a big buck on game purchases, the same way very few people spend money on hired professionals for text editing or photoshopping, since general purpose chatbots handle these tasks with ease under a monthly subscription. And thats the thing proponents of AI are promising, an age of abundance, where things we want are produced in excess and there are no shortages. I am highly skeptical it will occur on a full economy basis, but in the digital field it is highly plausible, and could materialize in the next 5-6 years. 

Lastly, people buy games for a shared experience, like a social network. If you make a game highly tailored to yourself, it is unlikely it will be popular among the masses. Likewise, you can easily build much better version of twitter or instagram these days, but with no people on it, it has no value. Same goes for the games , if it has a huge player base, it will still have some purchasing appeal.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Low value games you can one shot? No.

But if you think AI is, in our lifetimes, going to be able to whip up a polished GTA 6 from a single prompt... you're sorely mistaken. Yes, I think we'll get to a point where AI can make pretty much whatever you want, but not in a single prompt. And how many people are going to sit down and spend two years prompting their favorite model to produce all the features they want in their open world x rpg x   narrative-driven x choices matter game?

But yeah, I don't expect tetris and pac man copies to sell more than ten copies going forward.

comments.author: Specific-Heat-8553
comments.body: I wouldn't play or pay for anything here

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body: really? outside of vibe coded stuff, ai literally in any aspect bothers you?

replies.author: Specific-Heat-8553
replies.body: no ai doesnt bother me. I just havent gotten more than 1 minute enjoyment out of anything Ive tried out. If Im gonna play a game it has have a little more thought put into it.

comments.author: RatbyteGames
comments.body: I think down the track, its inevitable that AI will be not only able to produce a game on demand, but also movies, music and books for your consumption. "Give me a zombie apocalypse movie, where the hero has only one arm, and meets a border collie who saves his life and leads him to a sanctuary" then boom - the Ai will make if for you on the fly.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
That relies on me creating the world in my head from my own experiences and expectations. The whole fun of storytelling is to get something unexpected, that goes to places I couldn’t think of, that maybe nobody but the author has thought of.

There is an awful lot of derivative media out there and I’m sure it will continue to be churned out quicker and quicker by AI tools. The real content that moves a medium forward will always need that human spark.

comments.author: Dull_Mention_7456
comments.body: Not everyone has the time to iterate hundreds of times to make a good game.

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body: Of course, no one will pay for a low-quality slop created for a single prompt, either now or in the future. Creating a high-quality game requires a great deal of effort, even with the use of AI tools. Of course, no GTA-level game will be possible without a huge budget and years of development, either in five or twenty years, because by then, the requirements for creating AAA titles will have simply skyrocketed, a trend that has been evident throughout the history of game development.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
I have yet to see a vibe coded game I would like to play. The closest thing was a tetris clone.

I also have yet to see one of those vibe coded slop games to develop into anything more interesting and complete rather than getting thrown away, because they are unmaintainable.

comments.author: Nearby_Ad4786
comments.body: "I made GTA VI One prompt no mistakes"

comments.author: shoejunk
comments.body:
I expect the price of games to go down or the quality to go up. I think part of the appeal of a game is to play what other people are playing. Someone mentions a game or you see it on YouTube or Twitch and you want to play that particular game to have a shared experience with other players.

Also at least for now AI is bad at game design and bad at 2D and 3D animations. So humans with good taste and design sense still have a role to play.

comments.author: Coindk
comments.body:
I already do that with music, I'm creating the artists I want to listen to, I didn't discover any new artist in a while because I don't need to. There's that mystery box effect when you created something that sounds extremely good. The perfect track for you.

I'm working on great games I love too, I'll release most of them for free on my website for anyone to try them and/or copy them. This is how it the creative world works now, artists and creators should try to find new ways to create valuable things. Every human is an iteration.

comments.author: _TofuRious_
comments.body:
Depends on how you see video games, and why you consume them.

If you think video games are art, then you consume them for the specific experience/story someone else has catered for you. I think video games are art, and good art makes you feel something. And even with all this AI use I still think it's crucial that at the heart of a project there needs to be a human directing that experience so that the primary objective of making you feel something is there. As good as AI has gotten and will become I don't think it will ever know what is good inherently, it will always need a human to tell it if is good or not. AI also won't ever create something new, it always creates what is within it's data base. So I think there will always be a demand for new innovation with in the format.

If you just play video games as like a complicated fidget spinner then yeah you could probably replace all video games with what ever AI spits out for you on a whim.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
There is a huge market for hyper casual mobile games. I can see these being churned out by an AI in a day, rake in a few thousand dollars and then disappear into the App Store archives. Maybe this is where your vision fits. A player just says “I want to play Tetris but with machine guns” and they get something to entertain them for a few minutes.

Maybe it will get as far as doing this for AAA games. A player asks for “Call of Duty but with a disco theme” and they get a few hours of content, for a price.

There will always be a market for those who can craft an experience. This means finding enough commonality that many people want to do the same thing, but enough unique content that all those people will find something new while doing it. I can see this quest for authentic experiences becoming a key driver for game players in the future.

comments.author: Playistheway
comments.body: People can print whatever they want on card stock, yet people still buy Pokemon cards.

comments.author: ThickBootyEnjoyer
comments.body: I mean to some degree I understand what you're saying. But on the other hand, you're really over simplifying some things. If you want to play a game with your friends, and want to vibe code it. Then you're vibe coding it, then it needs to do the work which isn't quick. Then most likely you need to get your friend the game, hope there isn't network issues, and then get on together. IDK what kind of nights your looking at but my group is gonna be logged off way before any of that shit is finalized and figured out. Sometimes you just want a known quantity. Something you can download, load up, and it works.

comments.author: whimsicaljess
comments.body:
i will, at least: i don't care about games that are one-off personal experiences. i want games that i can play with other people and make friends by playing. 

i think we are just going to see an explosion of quality and content in games. indies will be able to ship games that feel like AAA made them, AAA will be able to ship at the speed of indies.

comments.author: vurt72
comments.body:
Define "games"? Its like asking if people are going to buy tap water at the store if they already have good tap water at home or tap water vs anything else that exists that you can drink.   
Indies, i think they might have a much harder time, but it will greatly depend on the genre and effort.

comments.author: pm_your_snesclassic
comments.body: Why do people still buy books when they can just write their own?
